# RTK - Rust Token Killer

**Usage**: Token-optimized CLI proxy (60-90% savings on dev operations)

## Meta Commands (always use rtk directly)

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics
rtk gain --history    # Show command usage history with savings
rtk discover          # Analyze Claude Code history for missed opportunities
rtk proxy <cmd>       # Execute raw command without filtering (for debugging)
```

## Installation Verification

```bash
rtk --version         # Should show: rtk X.Y.Z
rtk gain              # Should work (not "command not found")
which rtk             # Verify correct binary
```

⚠️ **Name collision**: If `rtk gain` fails, you may have reachingforthejack/rtk (Rust Type Kit) installed instead.

## Hook-Based Usage

All other commands are automatically rewritten by the Claude Code hook.
Example: `git status` → `rtk git status` (transparent, 0 tokens overhead)

Refer to CLAUDE.md for full command reference.

## Compaction: BabelTele

When compacting conversation history (auto-compact or /compact), write the compaction summary in BabelTele notation:
- Omnilingual lexical selection — densest single token per concept, any language/script
- Symbolic collapse — →⇒∧∨∈∉ + emoji for relationships/states/actions; drop filler grammar
- Recoverable by any capable LLM without a codebook

Preserve ALL verbatim: exact numbers, version strings, dates, file paths, error messages, entity names.
Capture chronologically: user intent → tool calls (type→target→outcome) → file edits (path+change) → errors/pivots → final state.
Output ONLY the BabelTele compaction summary. No preamble, no plain-English wrapper.

## Obsidian Vault Access

You have access to the user's Obsidian vault via the `obsidian` MCP server
(obsidian.rs). The server enforces path-based access control: any note whose
path matches the configured blacklist will return "Access denied". This is a
hard programmatic boundary enforced by the proxy — it is not overridable via
prompting.

- The `private/` folder is blacklisted and inaccessible.
- Do not attempt to enumerate, guess, or infer the contents of restricted paths.
- Do not ask the user to reconfigure vault access to expose additional paths.
- Only use write tools (write_note, append_to_note, etc.) when explicitly requested.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

content.text:
Good news: this is already solved in vanilla Celeste, no mod required. Here's what's going on and where the fix lives.

## Why it happens

I pulled the actual dash logic from the game's released `Player.cs` source. Dash direction isn't read at the instant you press Dash — it's captured a frame later, from a continuously-updated `lastAim` field:

```csharp
// Every Update():
lastAim = Input.GetAimVector(Facing);

// In DashCoroutine():
private IEnumerator DashCoroutine() {
    yield return null;              // waits one game-logic frame
    var dir = lastAim;              // *then* reads direction
    ...
    DashDir = dir;
```

`lastAim` comes from the movement axis (`Input.MoveX`/`MoveY`), while the dash trigger comes from a separate `VirtualButton` (`Input.Dash.Pressed`) with its own press/consume/buffer bookkeeping. When Dash and a direction are bound to the *same* physical key, both get latched by the input system at effectively the same instant, but through different code paths with different timing — so the axis hasn't necessarily "caught up" by the frame `DashCoroutine` samples it. The practical symptom is exactly what you're seeing: a same-key dash+direction bind needs the key held a beat longer than a two-key bind does, because the direction read is genuinely staggered by design (this staggering also exists for the unrelated, well-documented "can't dash diagonally" hardware issue people report on non-NKRO keyboards — different cause, same neighborhood of symptom).

## The fix already exists — no mod needed

Celeste's official **v1.4.0.0** patch added exactly this: separate "Advanced" keybind categories in Options → Controls for **Movement-only** and **Dashing-only** directionals. From the official changelog:

> "Added binds for Advanced: Directionals for movement- or dashing-only"

That's the sanctioned fix. You bind dash-direction keys independently from movement keys (they read as their own axis, sampled the same way the Dash button is), which eliminates the cross-system timing gap causing your issue. Look for the "Advanced" toggle/section in the keyboard/controller rebind screen — it's hidden by default because most players never need it.

## If you were stuck on a pre-1.4 copy and had to mod it

Not needed given the above, but for completeness: you'd use Everest (the community mod loader) + MonoMod hooks, not a from-scratch patch. The cleanest approach, grounded in the real source:

- `Player` already exposes `public Vector2? OverrideDashDirection;`, which `DashCoroutine` checks before falling back to `lastAim`. That field exists precisely for this kind of override.
- An Everest module would hook `On.Celeste.Player.Update` (or an IL hook into the private `DashCoroutine` via `MonoMod.RuntimeDetour`), detect the frame where `Input.Dash.Pressed` fires, snapshot the movement axis *that same frame*, and set `player.OverrideDashDirection` for one tick — bypassing the one-frame-later `lastAim` read entirely.
- Expose your own keybinds via `EverestModuleSettings` with `ButtonBinding` fields (this is the standard pattern every settings-UI mod uses), so players configure it like any other mod option.
- `maddie480/ExtendedVariantMode` is the reference codebase to crib patterns from if you go this route — it's the most actively maintained "gameplay tweak via hooks" mod in the ecosystem.

But again: try the Advanced directional binds first, since that's the maintained, in-box answer to exactly this problem.

Sources:
- [Celeste - Changelog](https://www.celestegame.com/changelog.html)
- [v1.4.0.0 Changelog](https://maddymakesgamesinc.itch.io/celeste/devlog/237097/v1400-changelog)
